run.note: PMF/FMF signal review of Lumen (home-energy monitoring, $6/mo consumer subscription). Question posed: raise a seed on the consumer-subscription thesis, or pivot to B2B white-label for utilities. Deliverable written; three checkpoint gates ride with it, none blocking.

findings.title: Acquisition is one unrepeatable event, not a channel
findings.statement: 71% of the 4,100 installs came from a single Reddit post, leaving a non-viral baseline of roughly 1,189 installs over 90 days (~13/day) as the only readable evidence of standing demand.
findings.impact: A seed investor underwrites repeatable acquisition. A viral post cannot be bought again, so the install total does not support the growth claim it is being used for.
findings.fix: Split retention and conversion by acquisition source, then buy a real CAC number against a defined segment (Test 1, Test 2).

findings.title: CAC is untested and is the first diligence question
findings.statement: With acquisition entirely organic, the company cannot answer the single number a seed investor asks first, and every unit-economics claim rests on it.
findings.impact: Walking into a seed meeting with no CAC figure ends the meeting regardless of how the other metrics read.
findings.fix: Spend $3-5k over weeks 2-5 against the solar segment to establish an order of magnitude, alongside a parallel price test.

findings.title: The $6 price sets a CAC ceiling near $19
findings.statement: At $6/mo net of a 15% store fee and an 11.1-month expected life implied by 9% monthly churn, net LTV is approximately $57, capping CAC near $19 for a 3:1 return.
findings.impact: A $19 blended CAC on a consumer utility app is a hard bar, making price rather than growth the binding constraint on the consumer thesis.
findings.fix: Test a $15-20/mo solar tier, which lifts the CAC ceiling to roughly $57 at the same churn rate.

findings.title: 22% D30 is uninterpretable until cohort-split
findings.statement: Holding the blend at 22% across a 71/29 viral-to-organic mix, a 15% viral cohort implies a 39% organic cohort while a 22% viral cohort implies 22% organic — two different companies.
findings.impact: The entire raise-or-pivot decision turns on a split that has not been queried, and the query takes roughly one analyst-day.
findings.fix: Run the cohort split by acquisition source and by solar vs. non-solar household before any other work.

findings.title: The 38% solar-export request is a segment disclosure, not a roadmap item
findings.statement: Solar-export tracking accounting for 38% of all feedback indicates that a large share of engaged users are solar households, a customer with prior five-figure energy spend and a live financial reason to monitor export against self-consumption.
findings.impact: Reframes the strategic question from consumer-versus-B2B to undifferentiated-consumer versus solar-household-consumer, and is the strongest available argument for a narrowed thesis.
findings.fix: Measure retention and churn for the solar sub-cohort before building the feature, and price-test a solar tier.

findings.title: The paid business is sub-scale and shrinking-capable
findings.statement: MRR is $1,260 (210 x $6, ~$15.1k ARR), and at 9% monthly churn with no new paid acquisition it decays to roughly $590 within eight months.
findings.impact: Revenue cannot fund the runway extension that either strategic path would require.
findings.fix: Treat revenue as evidence of willingness to pay, not as a financing option; plan the six-week evidence window against the eight-month runway.

findings.title: NPS 31 is survivor satisfaction and cannot arbitrate the decision
findings.statement: 140 responses against 4,100 installs is a 3.4% response rate from a self-selected pool of users who stayed, so the score measures survivors and does not predict retention or willingness to pay.
findings.impact: Using NPS 31 as counter-evidence against 9% churn would misread the dataset in the company's favor.
findings.fix: Exit-survey every cancellation from the last 60 days with one open-text question.

findings.title: Utility app ratings of 2.1 are not a consumer opening
findings.statement: Utility app store ratings largely measure the billing relationship rather than the software, so a 2.1 rating supports the B2B conversation but does not establish a consumer market opening.
findings.impact: The weakest inference in the current thesis; it will not survive diligence as a differentiation argument.
findings.fix: Use the 2.1 ratings only as the opener in utility conversations (Test 3), not as consumer-side evidence.

findings.title: The B2B pivot rests on no evidence and a sales cycle longer than the runway
findings.statement: There is no pilot, design partner, named budget, or pricing conversation supporting the B2B white-label option, and regulated utility procurement is committee-driven and budget-cycle-bound, plausibly exceeding the eight months of runway available.
findings.impact: B2B is fundable as a story but cannot function as a revenue rescue inside the current runway, so pivoting on the current evidence would be a strictly worse-supported bet than the existing path.
findings.fix: Falsify cheaply: seek one written pilot intent naming a budget line and a date from a municipal utility or rural co-op within three weeks.

assumptions.statement: Organic demand for Lumen exists independent of the Reddit post.
assumptions.basis: Only the ~1,189 non-viral installs over 90 days speak to this, and no paid acquisition has ever been run to price a marginal user.
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: There is no consumer business at any price; the raise fails at the first cohort question in diligence.

assumptions.statement: The 22% D30 and 9% monthly churn reflect a distribution problem rather than a value problem.
assumptions.basis: Assumed by the framing of the raise-or-pivot question; the same numbers are equally consistent with a curiosity-then-abandonment product.
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: Both strategic options fail for the same underlying reason, and a B2B white-label sells utilities the same abandonment at wholesale.

assumptions.statement: Lumen's hardware-free data supply is durable and not controlled by the prospective B2B buyer.
assumptions.basis: The brief does not state how consumption data is obtained without hardware; if it comes from utility accounts or smart-meter interval feeds, the counterparty in the pivot controls the input.
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: The moat argument disappears in diligence and the white-label pitch becomes an offer to sell a utility something built from data it already owns.

assumptions.statement: Subscriber life is 11.1 months, implied by treating 9% monthly churn as a constant hazard rate.
assumptions.basis: Arithmetic on the single blended churn figure supplied; real churn curves are usually front-loaded.
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: True LTV is higher than the ~$57 modeled, and the CAC ceiling rises accordingly; the direction of this error favors the company.

assumptions.statement: App store commission is the 15% small-business tier.
assumptions.basis: Not stated in the brief; assumed to compute net LTV.
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: At 30% every CAC ceiling in the deliverable drops by roughly a sixth, to about $16 at the $6 price point.

assumptions.statement: Solar households retain and convert materially better than the general install base.
assumptions.basis: Inferred from solar-export tracking being 38% of all feedback; never measured behaviorally.
assumptions.impact_if_wrong: The narrowed thesis has no segment behind it, the 38% is noise from a vocal minority, and the week-6 decision falls to the stop-or-sell branch.

gates.title: Which signal would actually change your mind?
gates.description: Thresholds proposed by this review (32% organic D30, 6% solar-cohort monthly churn, $19 and $57 CAC ceilings, one written pilot intent) are the reviewer's, not the founders'. The founders must pre-register their own kill thresholds in writing before the Test 1 query is run, or the result will be rationalized after the fact.

questions.label: Name, in writing and before the query runs, the organic-cohort D30 and solar-cohort churn figures you would accept as a kill signal.

gates.title: Stated pain conflicts with observed behavior
gates.description: Stated-pain reading: 38% feedback convergence on solar-export is unusually high consensus and retention is depressed because the product is incomplete for the users who care most. Behavioral reading: 22% D30 and 9% churn are what the whole population did, while 38% is what a vocal minority said. Falsification test: split retention and churn by solar vs. non-solar household before the feature ships. A second conflict, NPS 31 against 9% churn, is a survivorship artifact and is falsified by exit-surveying the last 60 days of cancellations.

questions.label: If the solar cohort retains no better than everyone else, do you still build solar-export tracking?

options.label: No — the cohort split is a real test and we abide by it
Yes — we would build it regardless
options.description: If so, the cohort split is not functioning as a test and should not be presented as evidence.

gates.title: Continue, narrow, or reposition?
gates.description: Raising, pivoting, and cutting are all one-way doors on an eight-month clock. The review recommends narrowing, but the decision depends on context the review does not hold: investor conversations already in flight, what the founders want to spend the next five years doing, and the personal cost of a wind-down.

questions.label: Which direction do we build the plan around?

options.label: Continue — raise on the consumer-subscription thesis as it stands
Narrow — run the six-week tests, then raise on the solar-household thesis (Recommended)
options.description: The review's recommendation; leaves 6+ months of runway and keeps the stop-or-sell branch open.

options.label: Reposition — commit to the B2B white-label play for utilities

recommendations.text: Narrow rather than raise or pivot: the evidence does not fund a consumer-subscription seed today and funds a B2B pivot even less, but it does fund six weeks of cohort and pricing work that could produce a fundable solar-household thesis.

Week 1, one analyst-day: split D30 free retention and paid churn by acquisition source (Reddit vs. organic) and by solar vs. non-solar household, and exit-survey every cancellation from the last 60 days. Pre-register thresholds first.

Weeks 2-5, $3-5k: buy an order-of-magnitude CAC number against the solar segment specifically, and run a parallel price test of the $6 tier against a $15-20 solar tier. Pass bar is CAC under the ~$19 ceiling at $6 or the ~$57 ceiling at $18.

Weeks 2-4, founder time only: take five conversations with municipal utility and rural co-op product owners. Pass condition is a written pilot intent naming a budget line and a date within three weeks; anything less falsifies the pivot under this runway.

If at week 6 the cohorts are flat and no utility will sign a pilot intent, take neither strategic option: cut to what $1,260 MRR sustains or pursue an acquirer while roughly 6.5 months of runway still provides negotiating leverage.

items.note: Delivered in lumen-pmf-review.html: the call, evidence audit, derived arithmetic, three load-bearing assumptions.
All nine supplied inputs graded in the evidence audit table against the commercial claim each is asked to support.
Three concurrent tests scoped to six weeks, each with a pre-registered pass or kill threshold.
gate-strategy, open, non-blocking; also raised in chat.
gate-conflict; both readings presented with one falsification test per conflict.
gate-direction, open, non-blocking; the review recommends but does not commit the founders to a one-way door.

items.item: No fabricated market stats, competitive intel, or interview quotes
items.note: Every figure derives arithmetically from the nine supplied inputs. Claims about utility procurement and incumbent app ratings are labeled structural argument, not cited statistics.
Findings carry a basis of reported or derived; six assumptions are recorded separately with impact-if-wrong.

items.item: Role boundary: no UX heuristic audit performed
items.note: Interaction-level critique is out of scope and routes to /ux-review; the deliverable notes the product itself was not inspected.

limits: Every figure derives from the nine inputs supplied in the brief. No external market data, competitor financials, category retention benchmarks, or utility procurement timelines were sourced or cited.
The product, onboarding flow, and paywall were not inspected. The 5.1% install-to-paid conversion and 22% D30 could be substantially explained by execution issues invisible to this review.
The cohort splits underlying every branch of the week-6 decision have not been queried; the load-bearing evidence does not yet exist.
How Lumen obtains consumption data without hardware is unstated in the brief, so moat durability and B2B negotiating leverage could not be assessed.
Subscriber life of 11.1 months assumes a constant hazard rate; the actual churn curve was not available.
App store commission assumed at the 15% small-business tier; at 30% every CAC ceiling drops by roughly a sixth.
NPS respondent composition (payers vs. free users, and when surveyed) was not available, so the degree of survivorship bias in the score could not be quantified.
No churn reasons exist in the dataset; nobody has surveyed users who cancelled.
The reviewer's proposed thresholds are judgment calls awaiting the founders' own pre-registered figures at gate-strategy.
